commands.name: alias
commands.summary: Create shorthand names for commands or command sequences.
commands.risk_reason: Non-persistent unless added to shell config; easy to undo.
cautions: Aliasing destructive commands (e.g. rm → rm -i) gives a false sense of safety — aliases do not apply in scripts or other shells.
commands.explanation: alias lets you define custom shorthand for long or complex commands. Aliases defined in the terminal session are temporary — to make them permanent, add them to ~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile. alias without arguments lists all current aliases.

examples.desc: Create a human-readable long listing alias
Shorthand for kubectl (essential for K8s work)

commands.pro_tip: Add `alias tf=terraform` and `alias k=kubectl` to ~/.bashrc — saves thousands of keystrokes per week.

commands.name: export
commands.summary: Set environment variables available to child processes.
commands.risk_reason: Scoped to current session unless written to shell config.
cautions: Exporting secrets puts them in the environment of every child process and (if typed) into shell history — prefer reading them from a file or a secrets manager.
commands.explanation: export marks a shell variable for export to the environment of child processes. Without export, variables are local to the current shell only. Used extensively in CI/CD pipelines, Docker, and application configuration. export -p lists all exported variables.

flags.desc: Remove variable from export list (don't delete it)

examples.desc: Set AWS region for CLI commands

commands.pro_tip: Use `export -p > session_vars.sh` to snapshot your current environment — useful before entering a complex debugging session.

commands.name: env
commands.summary: Print environment variables or run a command with a modified environment.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only by default; modified-env execution is scoped.
cautions: The environment often contains secrets (tokens, passwords) — do not paste the output into tickets or chats.
commands.explanation: env displays all current environment variables or runs a program with a temporarily modified environment. env -i runs a command in a completely clean environment — critical for reproducible builds and debugging environment contamination.

flags.desc: Use null separator instead of newlines

examples.desc: Run node with overridden env var

commands.pro_tip: Use `env -i` in scripts to avoid inheriting unexpected variables from the user's shell — production deployments should always control their own environment.

commands.name: printenv
commands.summary: Print the value of specific environment variables.
cautions: Variables may hold secrets — avoid printing everything in shared terminals, CI logs or screen shares.
commands.explanation: printenv prints the values of specified environment variables, or all variables if none are specified. Unlike env, it's purpose-built for querying — cleaner for scripting than parsing env output.

examples.desc: Safely check if a var is set

commands.pro_tip: In scripts, prefer `printenv VAR` over `echo $VAR` — the latter can be confusing if the variable contains special characters.

commands.name: source
commands.summary: Execute a script in the current shell context (no subshell).
commands.risk_reason: Changes affect current shell; sourcing untrusted files is dangerous.
cautions: Sourcing runs every command in the file in your current shell — only source files you trust and have read.
commands.explanation: source (or its synonym `.`) runs a script in the current shell rather than a subshell — so variables, functions, and aliases defined in the script persist after it finishes. Essential for applying changes to ~/.bashrc without restarting the terminal.

examples.desc: Reload bash config without restarting terminal
Load environment variables from a .env file

commands.pro_tip: Use `source .env` in dev workflows — keep secrets in .env (gitignored) and load them on demand rather than exporting globally.

commands.name: history
commands.summary: Display or manipulate the shell command history.
commands.risk_reason: Purely informational; editing history file requires care.
cautions: History files can contain passwords and tokens typed on the command line; `history -c` hides your trail but may violate audit policy.
commands.explanation: history lists previously executed commands with line numbers. You can re-run commands with !N (by number) or !! (last command). Ctrl+R provides interactive reverse search. HISTSIZE controls in-memory lines; HISTFILESIZE controls the history file.

flags.desc: Delete a specific history entry by number
Append session history to history file
Read new lines from history file

commands.pro_tip: Prefix any command with a space to exclude it from history — useful for commands containing passwords or tokens (requires HISTCONTROL=ignorespace).

commands.name: which
commands.summary: Locate the executable that would be run for a given command.
commands.explanation: which searches PATH directories for the specified command and prints the full path. Essential for diagnosing 'command not found' errors, verifying which version of a tool is active, and understanding PATH resolution order.

flags.desc: Print all matching paths, not just the first

examples.desc: Find all python3 installations in PATH
Verify terraform exists then check version

commands.pro_tip: Use `which -a <cmd>` when debugging version conflicts — it reveals all installed copies so you know exactly which one your PATH resolves to first.

commands.name: whereis
commands.summary: Locate binary, source, and man page for a command.
commands.explanation: whereis locates binary, source code, and manual page files for a given command, searching standard system directories (not just PATH). More comprehensive than which but less precise for custom installations.

examples.desc: Find bash binary, source, and man page
Find the systemctl man page location

commands.pro_tip: Use `whereis -b cmd` in automation scripts to check if a binary exists before using it — more reliable than `which` across different distros.

commands.name: tmux
commands.summary: Terminal multiplexer: manage multiple terminal sessions in one window.
commands.risk_reason: Sessions persist independently; easy to lose work if confused.
cautions: Detached sessions keep running (and keep any secrets or credentials in scrollback) — close them when finished.
commands.explanation: tmux creates persistent terminal sessions with multiple windows and panes. Sessions survive SSH disconnects — critical for long-running operations. Supports session sharing for pair programming and detach/reattach workflows.
commands.pro_tip: Essential keybindings: Ctrl+b d (detach), Ctrl+b c (new window), Ctrl+b % (split vertical), Ctrl+b " (split horizontal). Run long operations in tmux — they survive SSH drops.

commands.name: screen
commands.summary: Terminal multiplexer with persistent sessions (older alternative to tmux).
commands.risk_reason: Sessions persist after logout; orphaned sessions consume resources.
cautions: Detached sessions keep running and keep their scrollback — close them and avoid leaving root shells open.
commands.explanation: screen provides persistent terminal sessions that survive SSH disconnects, similar to tmux. While tmux is more modern and feature-rich, screen is often the only multiplexer available on minimal server installs.
commands.pro_tip: Inside screen: Ctrl+a d (detach), Ctrl+a c (new window), Ctrl+a " (list windows). Prefer tmux for new setups — screen is for when you're on a system without tmux.

commands.name: jobs
commands.summary: List background and stopped jobs in the current shell.
commands.explanation: jobs lists processes running in the background (&) or stopped (Ctrl+Z) in the current shell session. Combined with fg, bg, disown, and kill %N, it provides job control without needing PIDs.
commands.pro_tip: Use `disown -h %1` after backgrounding a job with & to prevent it from receiving SIGHUP when your session closes — a lighter alternative to nohup for already-running processes.

commands.name: sleep
commands.summary: Pause execution for a specified duration.
commands.risk_reason: Blocking; use carefully in production automation.
cautions: `sleep` in scripts is a race-condition workaround — poll for the condition you actually need.
commands.explanation: sleep pauses the shell for a given number of seconds (or minutes/hours with m/h suffixes on GNU sleep). Used in retry loops, rate limiting, and waiting for services to start. Often overused where proper readiness checks are better.

examples.cmd: for i in {1..5}; do curl -f http://app/health && break || sleep 3; done

commands.pro_tip: Replace `sleep 30` in startup scripts with a readiness loop: `until curl -sf http://localhost:8080/health; do sleep 2; done` — adapts to actual readiness instead of guessing.

commands.name: test
commands.summary: Evaluate conditional expressions in shell scripts.
commands.explanation: test evaluates conditions (file existence, string comparison, numeric comparison) and returns 0 (true) or 1 (false). Equivalent to [ ] syntax. The [[ ]] bash extension is safer and supports regex. The backbone of all shell script conditionals.

flags.desc: True if file exists and is a regular file

commands.pro_tip: Prefer `[[ ]]` over `[ ]` in bash scripts — it handles variables with spaces safely without quoting, supports `&&`/`||`, and enables regex with `=~`.

commands.name: declare
commands.summary: Declare shell variables with types and attributes.
commands.risk_reason: Scoped to current shell; -x exports to environment.
commands.explanation: declare sets variable attributes: -i for integers, -a for arrays, -A for associative arrays (hash maps), -r for read-only, -x for export. Enables type-checking and structured data in bash scripts.
commands.pro_tip: Use `declare -A` for config maps in bash scripts: store key-value pairs without external tools. Iterate with `for key in "${!map[@]}"; do echo "$key=${map[$key]}"; done`

commands.name: read
commands.summary: Read input from stdin or user prompt into shell variables.
cautions: Without -r, backslashes in input are interpreted; use `read -rs` for secrets so they are not echoed.
commands.explanation: read captures user input or reads lines from stdin into shell variables. Used for interactive scripts, parsing file content line-by-line, and prompting for secrets (with -s to disable echo). The -r flag prevents backslash interpretation.

flags.desc: Silent mode: don't echo input (for passwords)

examples.cmd: while IFS=: read -r user _ uid _; do echo "$user uid=$uid"; done < /etc/passwd

commands.pro_tip: Always use `IFS= read -r line` when reading file lines — prevents leading/trailing whitespace stripping and backslash interpretation that causes subtle bugs.

commands.name: set
commands.summary: Set shell options and positional parameters; control script safety.
commands.risk_reason: Disabling safety options (e.g., set +e) can mask script failures.
cautions: `set +e` hides failures; `set -x` can print secrets into logs.
Use `set -euo pipefail` at the top of scripts and understand its edge cases (||, if, subshells).
`set -- args` replaces the positional parameters.
commands.explanation: set configures shell options that dramatically affect script behavior. `set -e` makes scripts exit on any error. `set -u` treats unset variables as errors. `set -o pipefail` catches failures in pipelines. Together, they make scripts fail-fast and safe.

examples.desc: Enable all safety options (recommended at top of all scripts)
Enable debug mode: print each command before executing

commands.pro_tip: Start every bash script with `#!/bin/bash\nset -euo pipefail` — `e` exits on error, `u` catches unset variables, `pipefail` catches pipeline failures. This prevents 90% of silent script bugs.

commands.name: trap
commands.summary: Execute commands when the shell receives signals or exits.
commands.risk_reason: Misuse can suppress error signals and mask failures.
cautions: A wrong trap on EXIT/ERR can hide failures or run cleanup that deletes the wrong directory — quote and validate variables used in traps.
commands.explanation: trap registers commands to run when specific signals are received (INT, TERM, EXIT, ERR). Critical for cleanup logic: removing temp files, sending alerts on failure, and ensuring safe teardown of resources when a script exits.

examples.desc: Clean up temp files on any exit
Report error line number on failure
Ignore broken pipe signals (common in pipelines)

commands.pro_tip: Use `trap 'cleanup' EXIT` instead of duplicating cleanup at every exit point — EXIT fires on all exits (normal, error, signal), so one trap covers all cases.

commands.name: stty
commands.summary: Configure terminal line settings and fix broken terminals.
commands.risk_reason: Changing settings can make terminal unusable until reset.
commands.explanation: stty configures terminal I/O settings — baud rate, character echoing, special characters, and more. Most commonly used to fix a 'broken' terminal (no echo, garbled input) with `stty sane` or to set terminal size for remote sessions.

examples.desc: Reset terminal to sane state (fix broken terminal)
Set terminal size (useful in reverse shells)

commands.pro_tip: When a terminal goes silent (no echo after entering a password), type `stty echo` blindly and press Enter — this re-enables echo without closing the session.

commands.name: tput
commands.summary: Query and initialize terminal capabilities for scripting.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only terminal queries; terminal writes are temporary.
commands.explanation: tput queries the terminal database (terminfo) to retrieve capabilities like terminal dimensions, cursor control codes, and color codes. Used in scripts to produce colored output, move the cursor, and check terminal dimensions portably.

examples.cmd: RED=$(tput setaf 1); GREEN=$(tput setaf 2); NC=$(tput sgr0)
examples.desc: Define color variables for use throughout a script

commands.pro_tip: Define colors with tput in scripts: `RED=$(tput setaf 1); NC=$(tput sgr0); echo "${RED}ERROR${NC}: msg"` — more portable than hardcoding ANSI escape codes.

commands.name: parallel
commands.summary: Execute jobs in parallel from command line or files.
commands.risk_reason: Parallel execution can overload systems or APIs if not rate-limited.
cautions: Many parallel jobs can overload the machine or hit API rate limits — set -j explicitly.
File names with spaces/metacharacters need quoting (-q) — otherwise the wrong files are processed.
Test with --dry-run first.
commands.explanation: GNU parallel runs jobs concurrently across CPU cores or remote hosts, replacing xargs -P with a more powerful and flexible interface. Supports progress bars, retry logic, input from files, and running across SSH hosts. Essential for bulk operations.

flags.desc: Number of parallel jobs (default: CPU count)
Run jobs on remote hosts via SSH

examples.desc: Compress log files 8 at a time

examples.cmd: parallel -j 4 --progress kubectl delete pod ::: $(kubectl get pods -o name)
examples.desc: Delete pods 4 at a time with progress
Test endpoints with retry on failure

commands.pro_tip: Use `parallel --delay 0.1` when hitting APIs to avoid rate limiting — adds 100ms between job starts while still running many jobs concurrently.

commands.name: bash
commands.summary: GNU Bourne-Again shell
commands.risk_reason: Runs arbitrary commands; scripts execute with your privileges.
cautions: `curl … | bash` executes unseen remote code — download, read, then run.
Without `set -euo pipefail`, scripts continue after errors and can do damage with empty variables.
commands.explanation: The default shell on most Linux systems. `bash -c` runs a string as a command; `bash script.sh` runs a script.

commands.name: sh
commands.summary: POSIX shell
commands.risk_reason: Runs arbitrary commands; behaviour differs from bash.
cautions: `curl … | sh` runs unseen remote code.
Test scripts with the same shell they will use in production (shebang matters).
commands.explanation: On Debian/Ubuntu sh is dash; on RHEL it is bash in POSIX mode. Bash-only syntax ([[ ]], arrays) fails.

commands.name: type
commands.summary: Describe how a name is interpreted
commands.explanation: Tells you whether a word is an alias, function, builtin, keyword or file.

commands.name: command
commands.summary: Run a command bypassing functions/aliases
commands.explanation: `command -v name` is the portable way to test whether a program exists.

commands.name: eval
commands.summary: Execute a string as shell code
commands.risk_reason: Executes arbitrary text; injection risk with any untrusted input.
cautions: Never eval strings built from user input, filenames, network data or variables you did not set.
Prefer arrays, `declare -n`, or `printf %q` quoting over eval.
commands.explanation: Concatenates its arguments and runs the result as a command. Easy to misuse.

examples.desc: Typical safe use: apply output of a trusted program

safer.why: Quote values safely instead of eval

commands.name: exec
commands.summary: Replace the shell with a command
commands.risk_reason: Replaces the current process; the session ends when the command exits.
cautions: Typing exec in an interactive shell with a command that exits closes your SSH session.
commands.explanation: `exec cmd` runs cmd in place of the shell. `exec >file` redirects the whole script’s output.

commands.name: wait
commands.summary: Wait for background jobs
commands.explanation: Pauses until the given background jobs finish and returns their exit status.

commands.name: bg
commands.summary: Resume a job in the background
commands.explanation: Continues a stopped job in the background.

commands.name: fg
commands.summary: Bring a job to the foreground
commands.explanation: Moves a background or stopped job to the foreground.

commands.name: disown
commands.summary: Detach a job from the shell
commands.risk_reason: The process keeps running after logout.
cautions: Disowned processes lose their terminal — their output is lost unless redirected.
commands.explanation: Removes a job from the shell’s job table so it is not killed on hangup (-h keeps it in the table but ignores SIGHUP).

flags.desc: Do not send SIGHUP on exit

commands.name: unset
commands.summary: Remove a variable or function
commands.explanation: Deletes shell variables and functions. See the flags and examples below, and run `man unset` for the full reference.

commands.name: local
commands.summary: Declare a function-local variable
commands.explanation: Limits a variable to the current function in bash.

commands.name: getopts
commands.summary: Parse script options
commands.explanation: Parses short options in shell scripts. See the flags and examples below, and run `man getopts` for the full reference.

commands.name: shift
commands.summary: Shift positional parameters
commands.explanation: Drops $1 and moves the others down. See the flags and examples below, and run `man shift` for the full reference.

commands.name: mapfile
commands.summary: Read lines into an array
commands.explanation: Reads lines from stdin into a bash array — safer than word-splitting command output.

commands.name: time
commands.summary: Time a command
commands.explanation: Reports real, user and sys time. /usr/bin/time -v adds memory use.

commands.name: timeout
commands.summary: Run a command with a time limit
commands.risk_reason: Kills the command when the limit expires, possibly mid-operation.
cautions: Killing a command part-way (backup, migration, copy) can leave partial or corrupt output.
commands.explanation: Sends a signal (TERM by default) after a duration; add -k to follow up with KILL.

flags.desc: Send KILL after a grace period

commands.name: yes
commands.summary: Repeat a string forever
commands.risk_reason: Produces endless output and can fill disks or pipes.
cautions: `yes | command` defeats the confirmation prompt that is protecting you.
Redirecting to a file fills the disk quickly.
commands.explanation: Prints "y" (or any string) repeatedly — used to auto-confirm prompts.

commands.name: true
commands.summary: Exit with success
commands.explanation: Returns exit status 0; useful as a no-op or loop condition.

examples.cmd: while true; do date; sleep 1; done

commands.name: false
commands.summary: Exit with failure
commands.explanation: Returns exit status 1. See the flags and examples below, and run `man false` for the full reference.

commands.name: expr
commands.summary: Evaluate expressions
commands.explanation: Old-style arithmetic and string evaluation; $(( )) is preferred in bash.

commands.name: bc
commands.summary: Arbitrary precision calculator
commands.explanation: Calculator language; use -l for floating point.

commands.name: getent
commands.summary: Query system databases
commands.explanation: Looks up passwd, group, hosts and other NSS databases, including LDAP/SSSD sources.

commands.name: xdg-open
commands.summary: Open a file or URL with the default app
commands.explanation: Desktop helper to open files and links. See the flags and examples below, and run `man xdg-open` for the full reference.

commands.name: clear
commands.summary: Clear the terminal screen
commands.explanation: Redraws the screen; scrollback may remain. `reset` re-initialises a corrupted terminal.
